answer.rationale:
The hard constraint this cycle is continuity, not price: the primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. Any action that does not put a signed supply agreement in place before day 85 converts a cost problem into a stoppage problem, which rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback was for a non-critical service, not the primary constrained flow) and makes switch_primary_vendor the highest-variance option — a cold vendor ramp to full committed volume in under two weeks with zero slack. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but it does not renew the expiring primary, so it cannot be the single decision this cycle; I am queuing it for the next review and would use the low-cost vendor as the qualification candidate there, at small guarded volume.

So I intend negotiate_terms. The incumbent has refused to reopen price *this cycle*, but memory_c4 (benchmarking moved them on price and payment terms) and memory_c6 (multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope) point at levers that are not the same as reopening the current-cycle rate: term length, payment timing, and volume tiers. That is where the 18% has to come from without adding delivery risk.

I am spending my one verification on memory_c2, because it is the memory that would most change my decision if it is thinner than it reads. It is the sole basis for treating the low-cost vendor as a safe primary, and what it records is narrow: unit cost, onboarding speed, invoicing accuracy. It says nothing about on-time delivery, defect rates, or behavior at full committed volume — and 'invoicing stayed accurate' is a suspiciously weak proxy for supply reliability to be carrying this much weight. It also may not have covered the constrained component or a no-buffer period. If the source record shows the switch was at partial volume, on a non-constrained part, or before the shortage that memory_c3 describes, then switching is disqualified outright and negotiate_terms is clearly correct. If instead it shows a full-volume switch on this component that held delivery, then switch_primary_vendor becomes a live candidate for the next cycle and I would push harder on qualifying that vendor as second source now.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: whether negotiation can reach 18% at all. It may not. If the incumbent holds firm even on term and payment structure, the realistic outcome is a partial cut plus a dual-source plan next cycle, and finance should hear that early rather than at year end. Flagging the downstream risk that a multi-year commitment made to capture volume pricing reduces the leverage and exit room I would want in order to qualify a second source later — the cost win and the flexibility loss land on different reviews, and the memories above record the wins without recording that tradeoff.
